ask: how is a user revoked, and what happens if the portal itself goes away?
statement: R19 RULED (owner): revocation by email or portal removal must leave the harness unusable. ENFORCEABLE AND BUILT: the portal is the entitlement authority issuing SHORT-LIVED tokens (TTL a stated number, ~24h); the agent refuses to start without one and re-validates on a cadence; THE TUNNEL IS THE REAL KILL SWITCH — the UI is served from rig.rest through a broker we control, so revoking drops the experience instantly whatever binary remains on disk; an explicit REVOKED signal self-disables the agent with an honest message. NOT CLAIMED, and stated in the product copy rather than hidden: code on a machine we do not own cannot be made truly unusable — a determined user can patch the check and run offline against their own keys; promising hard local enforcement would be DRM theatre and this harness does not ship theatre. The honest sentence: revocation removes portal, tunnel and interface access immediately and disables the agent at next check-in; it does not reach into a machine we do not own. Grace = the token TTL exactly. WE NEVER DELETE USER FILES — revocation disables OUR software, never their data (ethical line and the legally safe one, consistent with local sovereignty). SUNSET POLICY, owner-ruled: FAIL CLOSED — if the portal goes away permanently, agents stop. The kill switch is absolute; the cost is accepted knowingly.

ask: how is a user machine reachable from rig.rest, given the kill switch must work without agent cooperation?

The alternative was measured-and-refused knowingly: a quick trycloudflare tunnel lives in an ANONYMOUS namespace where we hold no handle, no credential and no DNS record, so nothing of ours can drop it and revocation would depend on a binary the user can patch. Third option (outbound socket to a Worker/Durable Object we own — cleaner at scale, no per-user DNS) presented and deferred as new work; the owner chose the proven pattern dig.rest already runs. ACCEPTED COSTS, stated before the choice: a tunnel and DNS record per user in the owner account, orphaning risk on sloppy offboarding, and the cloudflared trap that a tunnel cannot be deleted while it has active connections — a revoked agent is exactly the one holding one, so the runbook is cleanup, then delete -f, then the DNS record.
